title: Musabaha
subtitle: Warm chickpea and tahini bowl
excerpt: Musabaha is the hot, chunky cousin of hummus: whole chickpeas bathed in a loose tahini sauce, finished with olive oil and cumin. It comes together in twenty minutes from tinned chickpeas and is eaten at breakfast or as a shared starter with warm pitta.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Foundational reference for Levantine mezze dishes, including musabaha and its variants. Sami Tamimi and Yotam Ottolenghi, Jerusalem (2012). Musabaha described as a breakfast staple in the Palestinian tradition.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The tahini sauce can be made up to two days ahead and kept in the fridge. Reheat the chickpeas and assemble just before serving.

content.text: Musabaha is a warm chickpea and tahini dish, served in a bowl rather than blended smooth like hummus. The chickpeas are whole and soft, the tahini sauce is loose and lemony, and the whole thing is eaten hot with a drizzle of olive oil and a pinch of cumin. It takes twenty minutes from start to finish with tinned chickpeas.

items.prepNote: two 400 g tins, drained and rinsed

content.text: You need a saucepan to warm the chickpeas and a small bowl to whisk the tahini sauce. Pitta bread alongside is expected.

Whisk {{tahini}} with the juice of {{lemon}} lemon and {{garlic}} of crushed garlic in a bowl. It will seize and look thick at first. Add cold water, a tablespoon at a time, whisking until the sauce is the consistency of double cream. Taste and add salt.
The sauce should flow off a spoon easily and taste sharp and sesame-rich. If it tastes flat, add more lemon juice.
Tip {{chickpeas-tinned}} into a saucepan with a splash of water. Heat over a medium flame, stirring occasionally, until the chickpeas are hot through, about five minutes. Season with salt.
Spoon the hot chickpeas into a wide, shallow bowl. Pour the tahini sauce over the top, covering most of the chickpeas. Drizzle {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} over the surface.
Scatter {{cumin-ground}} over the top. Add chopped parsley and chilli flakes if using. Serve at once with warm pitta.

items.symptom: The tahini sauce is gluey and thick
items.cause: Not enough water added during whisking
items.fix: Whisk in cold water a tablespoon at a time until it loosens to a pourable consistency.

items.cause: The tahini brand may be on the bitter side, or not enough lemon was added
items.fix: Add more lemon juice, a teaspoon at a time. A pinch of salt also rounds out bitterness.

items.symptom: The chickpeas are drying out in the pan
items.cause: Too much heat or not enough liquid
items.fix: Add a splash more water and lower the heat. You want them hot, not frying.

items.symptom: The dish looks split after the sauce hits the hot chickpeas
items.cause: Normal: the heat changes the texture of the sauce slightly
items.fix: Stir gently to combine. It should still taste good. Avoid making the sauce very far ahead.

content.text: Musabaha is eaten for breakfast across the Levant, from Beirut to Nablus to Amman. In Palestinian and Lebanese kitchens it often arrives before hummus at the shared table: the sauce is rougher, the chickpeas are whole, and the whole thing is warm. Street-food vendors in the old cities serve it from clay pots kept over charcoal, with fresh pitta torn and dunked straight in. The dish is sometimes called masabcha or m'sabha. The name comes from the Arabic root for swimming, which describes the chickpeas floating in the sauce.
